newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer sees German economy on steady growth path.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer sees German economy on steady growth path.

text.p: Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said on Thursday he expected the inflation-free German economic recovery to continue in 1997 and again signalled that he would welcome a small rise in the U.S. dollar.

Speaking to the foreign journalists' association in Bonn, Tietmeyer said the economic turnaround seen in the second quarter of this year appeared to have continued in the third quarter and seemed set to be maintained next year.
"We have found ourselves in a renewed upturn since the second quarter which continued in the summer months, albeit perhaps at a somewhat slower pace," Tietmeyer told reporters.
"I will not make a precise forecast, but I expect real growth of over two percent in 1997 without... a notable increase in inflation," he said.

Blaming a sharp rise in the German mark and high wage agreements for an unexpectedly sharp downturn in the German economy last year, Tietmeyer took pre-emptive action against a further rise in the currency by urging markets to buy dollars.

The dollar, which recovered steadily in the first half of this year after hitting an all-time low of 1.3450 marks in March 1995, slipped below 1.50 marks again earlier this week, sparking some concern that it could be on a new downtrend.
In his remarks, Tietmeyer welcomed the currency's recovery to above the significant 1.50 mark level.
"I consider it a welcome development and I would not mind if it were to go a little further," Tietmeyer said.
Turning to the interest rate outlook, Tietmeyer declined to give any clues on further Bundesbank monetary policy moves.
"For now I consider that they (interest rates) are appropriate, but we will continue to examine this," he said.

He added that there could be a further easing in long-term rates, over which the Bundesbank has no direct control, noting that this would depend on the financial markets continuing to have confidence that inflation would be kept low.
"The more the impression grows that European monetary union will be based on price stability, the greater the chances of a further reduction in capital market rates," he said.
Germany's discount rate was cut to an record low of 2.50 percent in April and money market rates, at around three percent for overnight funds, are also at an all-time low.
